15. The Secretary in the Department of Space informed the Committee that the 
Department of Space has activities which are primarily application driven related to the 
development needs of the country. Broadly, these applications are involved in two 
directions; one is telecommunication, television, broadcasting and meteorology. They are 
known as space based services, namely, INSAT system. Secondly, is a series of satellites 

called the Indian Remote Satellites that enable the acquisition of images over the land and 
ocean which are used in the context of agriculture and resource management. To 
complement the two systems is the necessary institutional framework estabJished over the 
years in the context of INSAT in regard to direction and the requirements for the future, its 
utilisation and review of utilisation-this is done by a high level Committee of Secretaries 
comprising of Secretary, Telecommunications, Secretary, Information & Broadcasting, 
Secretary, Science & Technology representing the three major services of the IN SAT 
system, i.e., telecommunications, television, broadcasting and the meteorological system. 
16. On the other side is a national natural resources management system for remote 
sensing. The management system has got a Planning Committee with the membership of 
Secretaries of user departments namely, Secretary, Agriculture, Secretary, Science & 
Technology, Secretary, Mines, Secretary, Water Resources who are all Members of the 
Committee. The Committee is chaired by Member (S&T) Planning Commission. 
17. In the area of Science, there is an advisory Committee of Space scientists consisting 
of some of the scientists from within the country who promote astronomy and oceanography 
in the country. They provide inputs to ISRO in the field of Space Science. After the 
Coordination Committee has persued these inputs, they get into specific missions known as 
Satellite missions. They are implemented by ISRO. 
As part of self-reliance there is a developmental programme which in totality carriers 
various activities to Indian industry. The R&D programme of the Government and its 
various departments help the industry to play their role. 
The Department of Space has the specific responsibility of completing the satellite to 
make it operational, satellite managing as well as corresponding infrastructural development. 
18. In the last one year, the Department had three major missions, one was of course 
successfully launched-INSAT-2C from French Guinea. This would be used for 
communication, television etc. INSAT 2C and other systems have been fully made into 
operational service. INSAT 2C togetherwith INSAT 2A and 2B launched in July, 1992 and 
July, 1993 respectively have 50 transponders which provide services to the DoT as well as to 
many other users. INSAT 2C was launched on 9th December, 1995, with the help of 
European Ariana Launch Vehicle. It is working satisfactorily. 
19. Self-reliance in satellite systems and launch capability has been important goal for 
providing cost-effective space based services on an ensured basis. The INSAT-1 series 
satellites were built by an American company to our design specifications. Subsequently, 
development of second generation INSA T satellites and Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) 
satellites were taken up in the country in tbe 1980's. The launch vehicle development was 
initiated in the early 1970's through SLV-3, followed by the development of Augmented 
Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV), and Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and 
Geosynchronous Launch Vehicle (GSLV), development is now in progress. 
20. IRS-1C .launched on 27th December, 1995 is the most sophisticated civilian remote 
sensing satellite in the world today. On board a Russian launcher, it has a Panchromatic 
Camera with 5.8 m and with resolution 70 kms. with stereo viewing capability. the LISS-III 
Camera provides multi-spectral data with a spatial resolution of 23 meters in visible in near 
infrared region and 70 meters in short wave infrared region, imaging the same region every 
24 days. Wide Field Sensor data with spatial resolution of 188 meters resolution is available 
every 5 days for the whole country. The constellation of IRS satellite include IRS-1-C, IRS-
1-B, IRS-P2 and IRSP-3 has become an international system recently with a US-based 
company entering into a commercial agreement with India for reception and marketing of 
IRS data world-wide. 
The satellite remote sensing applications using IRS system have proliferated into almost 
every facet of our national development and the data are now used regularly for agri­
cultural crop average and yield estimation, drought monitoring and assessment, flood. 

mapping, land use and land cover mapping, wasteland management, water resources 
management, marine resources survey and management, mineral prospecting forest 
resources survey and management. 
21. In the launch vehicle area, significant progress has achieved over the last three 
decades. The initial efforts were on the development of sounding rockets for space science 
experiments. SL V -3 provided capability to inject 40 kilogram class satellites into near-earth 
orbit. The capability was further built up through ASLV. The successful developmental 
flights of PSLV viz., PSLV-D2 of October 1994 and PSLV-D3 of March 1996 enabled India 
to place IRS-P2 and IRS-P3 satellites in the desired polar orbit. Thus India realised a 
capability to launch 1000 kg. class IRS satellites into polar sun-synchronous orbit . 
Development of GSLV for achieving indigenous capability to launch INSAT class satellites is 
progressing for the scheduled first developmental launch in 1997-98. Indigenous development 
of cryogenics engines and stages is making good progress. 
22. The major developmental tests would be completed by the end of this year. 
Secondly, realisation of the other systems is there. They are going to have the test for strap 
on motors. This is an upgradation of second stage liquid propulsion motor of PSLV . 
23. The next major effort on the GSLV is the procurement of the cryogenic stage. 
Under the current contract, it is a supply contract. The Russian agency, Glascomos, is 
delivering by the end of this year, the first of the flight stage of the Cryogenic for GSLV. 
The other things are, one ground mock-up stage. These are expected to be delivered some 
time in the next few months. As per the present planning, the realisation of the first 
developmental flight of GSLV is expected to be in early 1998. With the availability of the 
cryogenic stage by the end of this year as well as the realisation and tests of major sub­
systems and systems during this year, by the realisation of the remaining hardware for the 
flight model expected early next year. The mobile service Tower to PSLV at Sriharikota is 
being modified to launch the GSL V also. This mobile service Tower is 3000 tonnes, and is 
the largest moving system in the country. That is the kind of facility where the rockets are 
integrated. The modification of the mobile service tower is required to assemble 4 liquid 
propulsion strap on stages of GSL V and to take care to servicing the cryogenic upper stage. 
Other preparatory activities in Sriharikota are going on. They include facility for handling 
liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen which are primary fuels and oxidizer , powering the 
cryogenic engine, as well as other types of fuels which are needed for the lower stages. 
These handling systems as well as· monito ring controls have also been set up. The first 
development lanuch of GSLV is expected to be in the early part of 1998. 
24. On the application side, there are several applications of IRS data in hydrology, 
forestry and so on. The remote-sensing data is used by the Department of Agriculture for an 
early estimate of crop, one month before harvest. They want 90 per cent confidence and 
90 per cent accuracy. The satellite system is able to provide. On a specific question whether 
they coulc cover over 20% of the cropped areas, the Secretary informed the Committee that 
when the IRS-lC would come into the picture, they would be able to improve the capability 
of the existing system so that these areas could also be covered. The second major 
application, of course, is ground water. Ground-water exploration using geomorphological 
maps generation using Satellite Data enable . to identify ground-water. As of now, it is 
extensively supported by satellite imageries. They provide a good signature of the type of 
fields geo-lythology, where ground-water could now and charge subterraneous regions. Once 
these maps are available and analysed, they could come out with reasonably accurate 
assessments of ground-water. 
The most important application in the last 2-3 years is the Integrated Mission for 
Sustainable Development. Comprising the satellite imageries, assessment of water in the 

identified areas for ground-water and surface water as also the assessment of soil, s lope 
characteristic, vegetative cover and many scientific parameters relevant to management of 
water in a better scientific way and sustainability of water for agricultural and o ther type of 
activities · and a master plan which would specify areas growing rice, where water would 
deplete fast or how to arrest sand movement, etc. All these prescriptions which are specific 
to regions are identified. 
25. The other part is interesting, managerial arrangement to implement this which 
involves the local functionaries, district collector and others·as well as NGO's and people in 
the locality. They all participate once this information is available. And this has been carried 
out in six districts with visible results-Bhiwani in Haryana, Chandrapur in Maharashtra, 
Anantapur in Andhra Pradesh, Dharmapuri in Tamil Nadu. There are six districts, in which 
this has been done. In 15 districts it is under implementation. They have action plan for 174 
districts which is roughly 45 per cent of the areas of the country. These districts have been 
identified by the Planning Commission and also reviewed by the Department of Rural 
Development and the current priority areas for tile integrated mission for sustainable 
development are those identified by the Department of Rural Development 
and it has identified 94 watersheds to be immediately taken up for generation of action 
plans. They have already completed 54. The remaining are under progress. Scientific 
information from satellites i~ used for socio-economic development, to have geographic 
information system which is user-friendly. It is working satisfactorily. In the coming years 
one would see visible changes 'in many problem districts because of the scientific approach. 
The limited results currently indicate that there is very good potential in the context of 
developing many regions all over the country. 
26. India continues to play an important role in the international space fora including 
the UN Committee on peaceful use of outer space. A UN Asia-Pacific Regional Centre for 
Space Education has been set up in India and this is a recognition of expertise India has 
built and its role in sharing its experience in the development and application of space 
technology for societal benefits. 
27. The Asia Pacific U.N. Centre for Science and Technology education, is in operation 
for the last 6-8 months. It has started the first course and it is going on successfully. The 
important thing is that there are quite a number of regional competitors for this. Considering 
our ability to impart education in space science and its application and also noting the type 
of infrastructure we have created for this kind of job, the UN selected India to set up this 
prestigious Centre . Already 14 countries are represented in getting education in this are a. 
Twenty-six students are now participating in the course being conducted at Dehradun where 
the primary centre is located. 
So far as the budget requirements are concerned, it is Rs. 922 crores which comprises a 
Non-Plan component of Rs. 168.6 crores and a Plan component of Rs.753.4 crores. The 
original request to the Planning Commission was that their budget should be Rs.l,l35 
crores. The reason is, the overall VIII Five Year Plan share was Rs.3,5 00 crores. Out of 
this, they have roughly spent about half of it in the first three years of the Plan period. The 
remainder is what is supposed to be spent in the last two years of the Plan period. This 
being the last year of the Plan, taking into the total requirements and the milestones which 
have been made on which expenditure has already been incurred and is likely to be 
incurred, they requested for Rs.l,135 crores. Subsequently the Departm ent of Space 
reported its absolutely ess~ntial requirement of Rs.l,OSO crores. The Planning Commission 
had told them that they would get Rs.750 crores which was at the level of last year. This 
would essentially mean that some of their approved programmes which they have already 

committed and which have got ramifications in terms of services to the country in 
telecommun ications, televisio n broadcast, meteorology, remote sensing satellites, launch 
vehicles-it is a critical area for India-all these things would get affected and some other 
things might get delayed. Consequently, they did make a representation expressing their 
concern about the budget situation. The Prime Minister suggested to the Planning 
Commission to take a review of the budget requirements of the Department of Space 
keeping in view its critical importance. 
28. Regarding the implications of a budget pegged at Rs.750 crores, the Secretary 
mentioned the problems on continuing their contractual commitments on the cryogenic 
front. This was one area where they could have difficulties. The second, of course, was the 
upper cryogenic de velop ment which was a purely indigenous effort. This was going on a 
parallel basis. This is the kind of impact on the cryogenic technology programme which is 
·· being pursued based on our capability. Another area which was likely to be affected was 
the continuation of the PSL V programme. The subsequent launch of PLSVs might not be 
possible at the frequency at which they have been planned for launching them. They may 
fail to demonstrate that India was in the forefront in that area. Even the GSLV would get 
affected if they were to starve of funds because these were long-term programmes having 
international ramifications. The remote sensing satellite system was a system which was 
becoming a global system and it is critical for the national development. It is important for 
them to get as much as possible out of Rs.l,OSO crores which they have indicated as 
absolutely essential requirement. 
29. Starting with ARYABHATTA in 1975, experimental satellites such as 
BHASKARA-1 & 11, APPLE and ROHINI satellites were realised in the country by the 
eatly 80's. The INSAT-1 series satellites were built by an American Company to our design 
specification. Subsequently, development of Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) satellites, second 
generation INSAT-2 satellites and SROSS satellites were taken up in the country in the 
80's. The launch vehicle development was initiated in the early 70's through SLV-3 . This 
was followed by the development of Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle (ASLV) and 
Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV). Geosynchronous Launch Vehicle (GSLV) 
development is now in progress. Self-reliance in satellite systems and launch capability has 
thus been an important goal for providing cost effective space based services on an assured 
basis. 
DECADE PROFILE 
30. Asked in the context of decade profile (1990-2000) whether any mid-term appraisal 
had been done and any programme has been chalked out for the period beyond 2000, the 
Secretary infromed the Committee that the goals for the Indian Space Programme sought 
to be covered in the decade profile had been approved by the Space Commission and 
endorsed by the Planning Commission. The major programmatic elements of this decade 
profile were as follows: 
1. Sustain lNSAT System and IRS System on an assured basis and with enhanced 
capabil ities to meet the identified application needs. 
2. Operationalisation of the Space applications/services. 
3. Indigenous development of satellites and launch vehicles, interlocked with the 
application needs. Indigenous capability for SROSSIIRSIINSAT satellites and their 
launch from India through ASLV/PSLV/GSLV. 
4. R&D, technology development , applications development, experimentati on with 
new techniques. 

5. Infrastructure development to support the missions and programmes targeted for the 
decade. 
6. Advanced R&D to prepare for the pragrammes of 2000 AD and beyond. 
7. Maximal utilisation of industrial infrastructure and establishment of Space industry 
with appropriate linkages, . ·and 
8. Commercialisation/expo~ of Space services and systems. 
31. The Secretary apprised the Committee that the Annual Plan allocation of Rs. 753.40 
crores in 1996-97 which was at the level of 1995-96 and the Interim budget was grossly 
inadequate to maintain the tempo of the Space programme and also the contractual 
commitments with the international agencies, an enhancement of Rs. 300 crores atleast, was 
considered essential. The Department has · been informed that the Prime Minister has 
directed the Planning Commission to increase the allocation for DOS by atleast Rs. 150 
crorcs over and ubove the level of Interim b!Jdget, and that if the Planning Commission has 
difficulty in doing so, it may be taken up in September-October, 1996 for consideration in 
the Revised Estimates. 
The CommiUee recomends that adequate funding of the Department of Space is necessary 
not only to meet the requirement of the Space Programme and the bearing it has on vital 
ureas of national development but also to honour international commitments and contractual 
obligations. It is needless to say that the cooperation with internationaJ agencies is very 
ne<:essary in this prestigious field of national importance. The paucity of funds should not be 
allowed to stand in the way of the programmes. The Committee is satisfied with the directions 
issued by the Prime Minister to the Planning Commission and hopes that the t·esult of the 
review of budgetary allocation would be favourable to the Department of Space. 
1\fAJOR PROGRAIHMES 
IRS Satellites 
32. The Committee was informed that IRS-lC is the most sophisticated civilian satell ite 
in the world toady. IRS-lC provides multi-spectral data with a spatial resoluti on of 23 
metres invisible in near-infrared region and 70 metres in shortwave infrared region , imaging 
the same region every 24 days. Wide Field Sensor data with spati al resoluti on of lSS metres 
resolution is available, every 5 days, for the whole country. The panchrom atic datu with a 
spatial r esolution of 5.8 metres and stereo-viewing capability enables generation cf dig ital 
t crr~!i n models, better contour mapping and thematic mapping at 1:10,000 scale Earlier, 
lRS-l A followed by IRS-lB, IRS-lC and IRS-P2 satellites were realised and launched 
successfully. Another Satellite IRS-P3 has also been launched recently. T hese satellites ha\'e 
fonr.ed a unique constellation of operational remote sensing satellit es. 
This IRS constellation has become an international system recently, with a US-based 
•·Jm pany, EOSAT, entering into a commercial agreement with India for reception and 
i'·iarkc ting IRS data world-wide. 
:.alional Natural Resources Management System and Remote Sensing Applications 
33. National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS), instituted in the early 
80's seeks to ensure effective integration of the space systems , ground systems and 
application efforts during planning and implementation stage. 
34. The satellite remote sensing applications using IRS system have proliferated into 

almost every facet of national development and the data , were being used regularly for 
agricultural crop acreage and yield estimation, drought monitoring and assessment, flood 
mapping, land use and land cover mapping, wasteland management, water resources 
management, ocearvinarine resources survey and management, mineral prospecting, forest 
resources survey and management, etc. IRS has been the Integrated Mission for Sustainable 
Development (IMSD), launched in 1992. Under IMSD, action plans for sustainable 
development are generated for select water shedS/blocks in 174 districts in the country using 
data from IRS satellites and collateral socio-economic data. 
35. Regarding INSAT Satellites, the Committee was informed that INSAT-2A was 
launched in July, 1992, followed by INSAT-2B in July, 1993 and INSAT-2C in December, 
1995. These three satellites are, today, providing operational service for the country, along­
with the last of the first generation satellite i.e. INSAT-1D. The communication payloads 
on-board the first two satellites of INSAT-2 series viz. INSAT-2A and INSAT-2B comprise 
of 12 transponders in C-band, 6 transponders in extended C-band and 2 transponders in S­
band. These two satellites carry meteorological payloads consisting of a Very High 
Resolution Radiometer (VHRR) with 2 Km. resolution in visible band and 8 Km. resolution 
in infrared band. These satellites have transponder for receiving distress alert signals for 
search and rescue mission. INSAT-2C satellite, in addition to carrying the C-band and 
extended C-band communication transponders as in INSAT-2A and 2B, incorporates Ku­
band transponders for business communication, transponders for mobile satellite services and 
extended coverage of C-band transponder to enable TV programmes outreach beyond the 
India catering to the population from South East Asia to the Middle East. The International 
Telecommunication Satellite Organisation, INTELSAT, has entered into an agreement with 
India for leasing transponders from India's INSAT-2E on a commercial basis and accordingly 
additional capacity is being built into INSAT-2E which will also have an improved 
meteorological payload. 
36. The Committee was apprised that the INSAT System, established in 1983, is a joint 
venture of the Department of Space, Department of Telecommunications, the Indian 
Meteorological Department, All India Radio and Doordarshan. It represented India's first 
step towards implementing an operational Space System for identified national requirements. 
Besides revolution ising the telecommunication and TV telecast scenario in the country, the 
INSA T system has been used for educational TV programmes, radio networking, interactive 
distant education and training, weather forec.ast, disaster warning, business/data 
communication, satellite-aided search .& rescue and mobile communications. 
37. Educational television service through INSAT has been introduced both at 
university level in the national network in addition to primary school level in several States 
including Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Maharashtra, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh. A char1nel on 
the INSAT has been dedicated for development of education and training. This provides 
several interactive programmes in continuing education like programmes on development of 
women and children in rural areas, watershed development, training in Panchayati Raj, 
training for the staff of State Bank of India, etc. A two-year pilot project for demonstration 
of satellite-based developmental communication and training has been taken up in Jhabua 
district of Madhya Pradesh. 
38. It was further stated that the ground-based experiments, balloon-borne experiments, 
scientific pay-loads flown on sounding rockets and the recent SROSS satellite mission, have 
enabled India to make significant contributions in the area of Space Science. A number of 
nationally coordinated programmes in Space Sciences and the Universities have played a 
major role in this area. 
39. Besides , a major ground-based facility called Mesosphere-Stratosphere-Troposphere 

Radar (MST Radar) has been commissioned near Tirupati for research in atmospheric 
dynamics. 
The Committee was informed that PSLV is designed for launching 1000 Kg. class of 
remote sensing satellites into 900 Km. Polar sun-synchronous orbit. It has a lift-off weight 
of about 283 tonne and is 44 m. tall with four stages. The first stage is of 2.8 m. diameter 
and has 129 tonne of solid propellant. Six solid propellant strap on motors are attached to 
the first stage. The 2.8 m. diameter liquid propulsion second stage carries 37.5 tonne of 
propellant. The third stage is a 7.2 tonne solid propellant motor and the fourth stage is again 
a liquid propellant motor with 2 tonne of propellant. 
40. In the launch vehicle area, significant progress has been achieved over the last three 
decades. The initial efforts were on the development of sounding rockets for space science 
experiments. SLV-3 provided capability to inject 40 Kg. class satellites into near-earth orbit. 
The capability was further increased through the Augmented Satellite Launch Vehicle 
(ASLV). The two successful flights of ASLV, in May, 1992 and May, 1994, helped place 
SROSS satellites in near-earth orbits for space science experiments. The successful 
developmental flights of PSLV viz. PSLV-D2 of October, 1994 and PSLV-D3 of March, 
1996 enabled th~ country place IRS-P2 and IRS-P3 satellites in the desired polar orbit. India 
realised a capability to launch 1000 Kg. class IRS satellites into polar sun-synchronous orbit. 
Some more flights of PSLV have been planned for launching IRS series satellites. 
Development of GSL V for achieving indigenous capability to launch INSAT class satellites, 
is progressing for the scheduled launch in 1997-98. Indigenous development of cryogenics 
engines and stages was making good progress. 
41. Operational Satellites and launch vehicle systems call for a host of advanced 
technologies and multi-disciplinary development efforts, covering chemicals, materials, 
propellant processing, propulsion, aerodynamics, structures, mechanisms, inertial guidance 
and navigation systems, optical and inertial sensors, control systems, servo actuators, power 
systems, thermal control systems, data handling systems, transponders, high resolution 
imaging systems, systems engineering and mission management. The long lead-time required 
for development of these technologies to meet the stringent performance and reliability 
specifications for the space systems, call for initiation of developmental effort, well in 
advance. Focussed R&D and technology development activities were accordingly, taken up 
on a time-bound manner. • 
The Committee is satisfied with the progress made by the Department of Space in respect 
of the Space related programmes. The Committee is strongly of the view that the Space 
programme should not be allowed to stagnate. Adequate advance planning in this field in 
necessary and the Department of Space should go ahead in right earnest to plan its vision 
beyond the year 2000. To that end necessary goals and requirements of technology should be 
identified so that the programme does not suffer any set back. The Committee reiterates that 
the shortage of funds should not be allowed to stand in the way of space programmes. 
42. While the Committee seeks to ensure that the Department of Space is not starved of 
funds in order to carry out its space programmes, the attention of the Committee has been 
drawn to some of the audit observations in respect of Physical Research Laboratory (PRL), 
Ahmedabad, as have appeared in the Report of the Comptroller and Auditor General of 
India, for the year ended 31st March, 1993 (no. 6 of 1994). Some of these observations are 
reproduced below: 
- There were no norms for scientific, technical and non-technical staff requirements. 

As a result, an expenditure of Rs. 7.82 crores was incurred on excess 
supporting staff. (Para 10.1.2) 
- Out of 50 in-house programmes including 25 undertaken during 1987-93, only 14 
were completed and 36 were continuing at the end of 1992-93. Four programmes 
were ongoing for more than 10 years. 
- Out of 13 sponsored projects including nine projects undertaken during 1987-93, 
eight were completed. There was cost overrun ranging from Rs. 1.15 lakhs to Rs. 
61.50 lakhs and time overrun of 12 months to 50 months in these completed projects. 
- In April 1976, PRL decided to set up an infra red telescope (IRT) at Mount Abu for 
research purposes at a total cost of Rs. 52 lakhs. The cost was revised to Rs. 192.44 
lakhs in December, 1984. Even after 16 years and spending Rs. 367.16 lakhs, IRT 
has not been Commissioned. Department of Electronics (DoE) entrusted the 
project: 'Appropriate Automation Promotion Programme' (AAPP) to PRL in 
January, 1984 for automation of textile industry. This was not within the purview of 
PRL as PRL's main objective was to conduct research in space science for DoS. The 
project had not been completed even after nine years and spending Rs. 199.92 lakhs 
by DoE against the estimated period of five years. 
- Department of Science and Technology (DST) approved a project in April, 1977 for 
setting up of Inter-planetary Space. (IPS) stations at a cost of Rs. 27.76 lakhs for a 
period of six years. Although three stations at Thaltej (Ahmedabad), Surat and 
Rajkot were set up at a cost of Rs. 40.11 lakhs, and with delay of three years, the 
Surat station was closed in April, 1992 and the Rajkot station was not giving 
continuous data. Thus, due to closure-non-working of the two IPS stations 
expenditure of Rs. 27.40 lakhs on their setting up had proved unfruitful. The fate of 
the third station at Thaltej is also uncertain due to radio broadcast interference. 
- Department of Commerce, United States of America approved a project: 
'Coordinated Studies of Solar X-ray and optical wave length and travelling inter­
planetary phenomenon during s9lar maximum year and beyond' in April, 1987 at a 
cost of Rs. 89.90 lakhs for a period of five years. The objectives of the project to 
collect data from 1000 stellar radio sources and transfer of IPS data to USA had not 
been achieved even after lapse of six years and spending Rs. 92.95 lakhs. 
- DST approved a project: 'Faint Object Astronomy with charged Coupled Devices 
(CCD) Camera' in August, 1984 at a total cost of Rs. 16.22 lakhs for a period of 
four years. Although PRL developed a CCD camera at total cost of Rs. 23.63 lakhs 
with a delay of more than two years, the ultimate objective of use of CCD camera in 
Indian telescopes had not been achieved. (Para 10.1.6) 
- Physical verification of stores at PRL and other subsidiary units at Mount Abu, 
Udaipur and Thaltej had not been conducted since inception. (Para 10.1.8) 
- Due to non-investment of excess funds in term deposit, PRL incurred loss of interest 
of Rs . 1.09 crores. (Para 10.1.HJ) 

The above list is only illustrative and not exhaustive. 
While appreciating the work and performance of the Department of Space, the 
Committee would like the Depar tment of Space to attend to the audit observation in respect 
of the Physica l R esea rch Laborato ry, Ahmedabad. The Committee may be apprised of the 
action taken in the matt er .

approved.

towards realising the Gaganyaan Programme, the Department had projected an amount of Rs. 4,256.78 
crore in BE 2020 -21, against which an amount of only Rs.1,200 crore has been  allocated.

6. INDIAN INSTITUTE OF SPACE SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY (IIST) 
6.1 The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Science and Technology, 
Environment, Forests & Climate Change  during its study visit to Thiruvananthapuram, Chennai, 
Sriharikota, Bengaluru and Ahmedabad from  26th to 30 th December, 2019 , held detailed discussion 
with the Director, IIST on the activities and functioning of the Institute on 26 th December, 2019 at 
Thiruvananthapuram. The Committee noted that the Institute is an autonomous body under the 
Department of Space, and was established in 2007 with the objective of offering high quality education 
in space science and technology to meet the demands of the Indian Space Programme. 
6.2 The Committee learnt that the Inst itute offers undergraduate, postgraduate, doctoral and  post-
doctoral programmes in the broad areas of space science, technology and applications.   It was brought 
to the notice of the Committee that the Institute carries out cutting edge research and development in 
space studies, and acts as a think-tank to explore new directions for the Indian Space Programme.  It is 
also gratifying to note that an overwhelming majority of the graduates have joined ISRO itself.   The 
Committee is, therefore, of the view  that given its mandate and its impact so far , the Institute 
must be immediately granted the status of ‘Institute of National Eminence’ through an act of 
Parliament.

8. CONCLUDING OBSERVATIONS  
The Committee had visited  a number of ISRO facilities in Thiruvananthapuram, 
Sriharikota, Bengaluru and Ahmedabad in December 2019.  The visit was a great educational 
experience for all members, and the Committee would like to highlight the following: 
(i) Efforts to indigenise electronic components in our space programme must be 
intensified, if needed in Public Private P artnership (PPP) mode . An import 
dependence of more than 80% is unacceptably high.  
(ii) The country's space programme depends on a single foreign company for the entire 
supply of carbon fibre and composites.  This is an area that demands urgent attention  
of the government. 
(iii) ISRO's R&D and academic outreach programmes are still heavily focussed in the 
southern part of the country and with elite institutions.  Better coverage is needed in 
the eastern and north-eastern regions of the country as well. 
(iv) ISRO's launch facility at Sriharikota needs substantial upgradation of access and 
logistics infrastructure, particularly since the number of annual launches is projected 
to double in the next five years.  The launch facility has a coastline of around 50 kms , 
which requires the highest level of maritime security. 
(v) It is recommended that Sullurpet should be developed as a smart city which will 
benefit the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Srikarikota as well. 
(vi) ISRO’s takeover of the Semi -Conductor Laboratory at Chandigarh is a m ajor step 
forward and while microprocessor design capabilities have now been proven, the 
marked absence of micr oprocessor fabrication and manufacturing facilities does no 
merit to our country, which is a world power in Information Technology. Such 
facilities must be established in PPP mode, if need be, with international collaboration.

Rs.4,295.44 crore for BE 2020 -21, against which an amount of Rs. 3100 crore has been allocated.   The

2.4 The Committee asked the Ministry about the bare minimum increase required in the budgetary

they require at least Rs.600 crore additional funds to sustain its key programmes/schemes during the

additional funds is most necessary are ‘Control of Pollution’ (National Clean Air Programme) –

‘Control of Pollution’ duri ng 2020 -21 instead of Rs.660 crore projected by them.  It was going to

2.5 The Committee is of the view that both the above programmes, especially National Clean 
Air Programme, are of utmost import ance in the present day context, and controlling air 
pollution must be given the topmost priority.  The allocation of additional funds would help 
support additional 22 non -attainment cities under ‘Control of Pollution’ scheme.  The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry must be provided the requisite allocation as 
sought by the Ministry with respect to these two programmes at the RE stage. 
3. ALLOCATION FOR CONTROL OF POLLUTION TO MoHUA 
3.1 The Committee pointed out that the Finance Minister has announced Rs. 4400 crores for clean 
air for large cities having population above one million  in her Budget Speech.  The Ministry informed 
the Committee that the said Fund is being made available to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs 
(MoHUA). The Committee desired to know how the Ministry would align its ‘Control of Pollution ’ 
scheme with the fund allocation to MoHUA in order to meet its shortfall.   Elaborating on the issue, the 
Ministry informed that the b udgetary allocation of Rs 4400 crore through MoHUA, is intended to be a 
performance related grant , which would be released to only the m illion plus cities based on the 
improvements in average annual concentrat ions of both PM 10 and PM2.5 ( equal weightage of 50%). 
Such grant would, however, be released only based on the improvements (as calculated in  Jan 2021). 
Cities shall utilis e the same for taking up activities/ measures that would help to bring  down the 
pollution levels further. National Clean Air Program (NCAP) component under the ‘Control of 
Pollution’ Scheme would take up measures in all the 102 non -attainment cities (initi ally identified). 
This number has increased to 122 non- attainment cities (76 cities with non-million plus population). In 
the year 2020 -21, additional cities are to be supported to take up the measures for the abatement and 
control of air pollution.   Thus, allocation of funds under ‘Control of Pollution ’ Scheme would help 
support non-million plus non-attainment cities. It would also help support the million plus non-attainment 
cities in 2020-21, before these cities may receive funds in the last quarter based on their improvements in 
PM 10 and PM 2.5 levels. 
3.2 The Committee observes that the allocation of  Rs.4,400 crore for pollution control to 
Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs is more than the entire budget allocation for 2020 -21 for 
the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The Committee notes that there are 46 
cities in India, with a population above 1 million.  The Committee recommends that these 46 
cities can be kept out of the 102 non-attainment cities identified by the Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change to take up measures for the abatement and control of air pollution .  
This would also help the Ministry reduce the shortfall of funds being sought by them for their

5. UTILISATION OF CAMPA FUND 
5.1 During the meeting, the Committee brought to the notice of the Ministry the instances of the 
CAMPA fund not being utilised properly in some states.  The Committee also noted that CAMPA fund 
had a huge corpus of Rs.54394 crore.  Noticing that the Ministry h ad indicated shortfall in allocation in 
some of its key schemes/programmes, the Committee desired to know whether the Ministry could 
dovetail the CAMPA fund with its other activities/programmes so that the pressure on the General 
Budget could be reduced.   
5.2 In response, the Ministry informed the Committee that as per the Compensatory Afforestation 
Fund (CAF) Act, 2016, National and State Funds have been established under the Public Account of 
India and the Public Account of States in which monies receive d from user agencies towards 
compensatory afforestation, additional compensatory afforestation, penal compensatory afforestation, 
net present value and all other amounts recovered from such agencies under the Forest (Conservation) 
Act, 1980 are credited. These funds are basically compensatory levies arising out of non-forestry use of 
forest land or protected areas for developmental needs of the country. These compensatory levies have 
primary role in mitigating impact of loss of tree cover, forest land, wild life habitat and ecological 
services rendered by the forests.  The monies in the National and State Funds can be utilised as per 
provisions of CAF Act, 2016 and CAF Rules, 2018.  T here is no specific provision in the CAF Act, 
2016 to fund any other scheme of the Ministry from the National Fund. The schemes can only be 
funded as per Section 5 (b) (iii) of CAF Act, 2016. 
5.3 Responding to the issue raised regarding the improper utilisation of the CAMPA fund, the 
Ministry apprised the Committee of the mechanis m for ensuring appropriate utilisation of CAMPA 
fund.  The Committee was informed that a monitoring group has been constituted as per Section 9 (iii) 
of the CAF Act, 2016. The major functions of the monitoring group (Section 16 of CAF Act, 2016) 
include evolving independent system for concurrent monitoring and evaluation of works implemented 
in States and Union Territories; inspection and undertaking financial audit of funds released by the 
National Authority; and devising measures for transparency and acco untability. Monitoring protocol 
for afforestation works under CAMPA is being developed by the Forest Survey of India, which is 
based on remote sensing data and analysis of satellite imageries with ground truthing.  In addition to 
this, the State Authoritie s are at liberty to carry out internal monitoring as well as third party 
monitoring and evaluation of works carried out through CAMPA Funds.  
5.4 The Committee observes that CAMPA is a huge fund.  However, its guidelines have been 
drafted in such a manner that its resources cannot be used for the schemes/programmes of the 
Ministry with similar objectives where it requires the money most.  The Committee is of the view 
that CAMPA funds have accumulated due to deforestation.  There is, therefore, no reason tha t 
the Green India Mission, which primarily aims at afforestation, cannot be funded out of the 
CAMPA fund.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and 
Climate Change should explore the possibility of allocating CAMPA funds for tho se 

6 
 
schemes/programmes of the Ministry having similar objectives as envisaged in the activities to be 
undertaken by the CAMPA fund, even if it requires amendment to the CAMPA Act/Rules and 
the Committee would support the Ministry in this matter.  This would  also, to an extent, reduce 
the financial burden on the Ministry and it would be able to utilise the fund for its schemes with 
similar objectives. 
6. Green India Mission - National Afforestation Programme 
6.1 The Committee was informed that National Afforestation Programme (NAP) was merged with 
Green India Mission scheme for budgetary allocation during 2018 -19 & 2019 -20.  Budget s were 
allotted to both the Green India Mission and NAP scheme to the tune of Rs.157.50 crore for 2018 -19 
and Rs.140.00 crore  for 2019-20.  Out of  the allocated budget, an expenditure of Rs.95.38 crore was  
incurred during 2018-19 for taking up new affores tation activities over 16636 ha and an expenditure of 
Rs.21.98 c rore has been incurred during 2019 -20, till date , for new  afforestation over of 19724 ha,  
including maintenance of previous year’s plantation and nursery work. 
6.2 The Committee acknowledges that the National Afforestation Programme is one of the 
important programmes of the Government for protection and conservation of natural resources

better management and conservation  of natural resources. R&D programme has funded 16 projects

8. MAN-ANIMAL CONFLICT 
8.1 During the meeting, the Committee enquired about the man -animal conflict and the 
compensation to be granted in case of human/animal loss.  The representatives of the Ministry 
informed the Committee that there is a component of a scheme, which deals with wi ldlife conflicts.  It 
involves minimising wildlife conflict by taking up such activities because of which the habitat is 
improved and the wild animal does not come out of the habitation.  In response to a query about the 
compensation, the Ministry stated t hat they provided financial assistance to States/UTs under various 
Centrally Sponsored Schemes, for ex gratia relief at the following rates:

Rs.15 lakhs.  With regards to cattle getting killed, Odisha was paying Rs.10,000 whereas Maharashtra 
was paying Rs.50,000.  The Committee was further informed that in order to compensate the damage 
caused to the crops by wild animals, the Ministry has brought this loss under the Pradhan Mantri Krishi 
Bima Yojana. 
8.3 While deliberating on the subject, the Committee brought th e instances of revenge killing of 
animals by the affected parties to the notice of the Ministry.  The Committee also enquired about the 
measures taken for p revention of deaths/injuries arising out of Man -Elephant conflict in the country.  
The Ministry informed the Committee about the following measures taken by them in this respect: 
(a) Financial and technical assistance is provided to elephant range states under ‘Project 
Elephant’, to protect elephants, their habitat and corridors;  
(b) Ex-gratia relief in case of human death/injury and property/crop loss; 
(c) Notification of critical elephant habitats as Elephant Reserves for better management 
of wild elephants; 
(d) All the elephant states have been directed to implement Guidelines for Management of 
Human-Elephant Conflict; and   
(e) Wildlife Institute of India , in consultation with MoEF&CC, National Highway 
Authority of India, National Tiger Conservation Authority  and World Bank Group has 
published a document namely ‘Eco -friendly Measures to Mitigate Impacts of Linear 
Infrastructure’ to assist project agencies in designing linear infrastructure in a manner 
that reduces human-animal conflicts. 
8.4 The Committee notes the compensation available for human/cattle/crop loss in case of 
man-animal conflict and the financial assistan ce provided by the Ministry of Environment, 
Forest and Climate Change to the States/Union Territories in such cases .  The Committee 
observes that the amount of compensation varies a lot from state to state.  The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change must take initiative 
to carry out a comprehensive review of the compensation  being provided in different states and 
frame guidelines to align the compensation at an equiv alent and realistic level , so that the 
affected persons are suitably compensated for the loss suffered by them  equitably all over the 
country. 
8.5 The Committee also takes a serious view of the cases of revenge killing of animals by the  
affected persons.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry must impress upon the State 
Governments/Union Territories to ensure that prompt payment of compensation is made to the 
persons affected by man -animal conflicts  on time , which would deter people  resorting to 
retaliatory killing of wild animals.

9.1 During the meeting, the Committee also raised the issue of plantation of a very large number of

large number of plants also required proportionately large tracts of land and expressed apprehension of 
money being siphoned off in such cases.  The Committee also called for the audit of the plantation 
activities. Responding  to this, the Ministry informed the Committee that National Afforestation 
Programme is monitored at the village level by the members of JFMCs by way of social auditing at 
district level by Forest Development Agency (FDA) and at the State level by State For est Development 
Agency (SFDA).  The Ministry also monitors the implementation of the scheme through Utilisation 
Certificates, Quarterly physical and financial Progress Reports (QPRs). The audit report and the 
statement of Accounts of previous year, duly audited by a Charted Accountant in the panel of C&AG is 
a pre -requisite for sanctioning grant. The afforestation sites are periodically evaluated by the State 
Forest Department and the Ministry by engaging independent evaluators having credibility and 
expertise. The concurrent evaluation of plantation is also carried out in the 3 rd and 5th year of the five 
year plantation cycle by SFDA.

apprehension expressed by the members cannot be ruled out.  The Committee recommends that

5. WEATHER FORECASTS/RAINFALL VARIABILITY AND CHANGES 
5.1 The Committee enquired from the Ministry about the steps taken by the Ministry to improve 
the accuracy of weather forecasts and to bring it at par w ith the International standards.   The 
Committee was informed by the Ministry that India Meteorological Department (IMD) is dedicated 
for monitoring, detection and forecasting of weather and climate including early warning for severe 
weather events such as cyclones, heavy rainfall etc. Th e weather forecasting and early warning 
systems in the country are comparable to most of the developed countries in the world in terms of 
accuracy, lead time and associated impact. Over the past few years, the quality of weather & 
climate services provided  by the M inistry has improved due to systematic efforts in augmenting 
atmospheric observations developing adequate modelling strategy, conducting cutting edge research 
and investing in human resources development.  IMD continuously expands its infrastructu re for 
meteorological observations, data exchange, monitoring & analysis, forecasting and warning 
services using contemporary technology. IMD uses a suite of quality observations from Indian and 
International satellites, radars and conventional& automatic weather stations for monitoring and 
prediction of weather. The High Performance Computing (HPC) systems have been recently 
upgraded by 6.8 petaflops so as to support the ongoing efforts on modelling. Operational 
implementation of improved suite of predicti on models has enhanced the weather forecasting 
capability through assimilation of all available global satellite radiance & Radar data for the 
generation of forecast products at 12 km grid globally  and 3 km grid over India/regional/mega city 
domains. 
5.2 The Committee was further informed that under the National Monsoon Mission program, 
advanced dynamical prediction systems have been developed for Seasonal prediction of Monsoon; 
Extended range prediction (for next 20 days) and Short & medium range (up to 10  days) weather 
prediction.  In addition, a high resolution (12 km grid scale) state of the art Global Ensemble 
Prediction System (EPS) was commissioned on 01 June 2018, which is one of the best in the world. 
The Ensemble forecasts will enhance the weather information being provided by the current models 
by quantifying the uncertainties in the weather forecasts and generate probabilistic forecasts. 
5.3 During the meeting of the Committee held on the 17 th February 2020, many Members of the 
Committee raised serious concerns  about the changing rainfall p attern in their respective 
constituencies/States, which had adversel y affected the local population and the crops of farmers.  
The members observed that sometimes, their respective areas suffer from dry days and there is not 
enough water for the farme rs.  At other times, there is heavy rainfall, which damages the crops.  
Both the se situations are harming farmers significantly.  Members also noted  the rise of sudden 
downpours or cloudbursts in their respective states.  The Secretary of the Ministry, informed the 
Committee that the Ministry has prepared a report on Observed Rainfall Variability and Changes to 
find recent changes in the rainfall pattern over 28 states and one UT i.e. Jammu & Kashmir base d 
on the data of the last 30 years (1989-2018), as desired by the Committee in its last meeting held 
with the representatives of Ministry of Earth Sciences in September 2019.   The rainfall pattern of 
monsoon months, south west monsoon season , and annual rainfall of the State and its districts as 
well as extreme rainfall event of different intensity of stations have been analysed in the report.  

9 
 
While apprising the Committee of the significant trends in the State Rainf all, the Secretary of the 
Ministry brought out the following: 
• Five States viz. Bihar, Meghalaya, Nagaland, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh have shown 
statistically significant decreasing trends in Southwest monsoon rainfall. 
• All these five states along with two more states viz. Arunachal Pradesh and Himachal 
Pradesh have also shown statistically significant decreasing trends in annual rainfall. 
• However in the district rainfall, significant changes have been noticed for most of the states. 
5.4 The Ministry also informed the Committee  that there had been significant changes in the 
frequency of dry days, rainy days (daily rainfall of 2.5 mm or more but less than 7 cm) and heavy 
rainfall events (rainfall greater than equal to 7cm).  Further, it was also pointed out that the situation 
for agriculture or water recharges in the states in the Ganga basin viz. Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar 
and West Bengal and some states of extreme south peninsula is alarming, as the number of dry days 
during southwest monsoon is significantly increasing and als o the frequency of rainfall of lower 
intensities (less than 7 cm) favourable for soil and ground water recharges is decreasing over these 
regions.   
5.5 The Committee desired to know whether the Ministry could predict sudden cloudbursts.  In 
response, the Secretary responded that they can make prediction two hours before  such extreme 
events. He also stated that they termed cloudbursts as heavy rains with ten centimeters or more in 
one hour. However, it does not happen very often. In their written reply on the subject, the Ministry 
further stated that c loud bursts are being predicted in now cast mode, i.e, 2 -3 hours in advance in 
terms of heavy rainfall using Doppler Weather Radars and Satellite Data.  
5.6 The Committee further des ired to know from the Ministry that if the Ministry received 
requisite funds, whether it is possible to predict a cloudburst 3 days in advance.  The Ministry stated 
that with the existing super computer, they are able to run global weather prediction models with a 
horizontal resolution of 12km. The proposed supercomputing system will be able to reduce the 
12km grids down to 5 km, giving far more detailed predictions. It was further stated that unlike 
cyclones, forecasting a  cloudburst is very difficult due to the dynamics of the rapidly developing 
clouds over a very small area. However, they could make a probabilistic fo recast on possibility of 
cloudburst events over a specific area 48 hours in advance with enhanced computing facility.  
5.7 The Committee and the Chairman enquired the amount of expenditure allocated to the 
overall study and prediction of the monsoon and its changing patterns. The Se cretary informed the 
Committee that approximately 30 percent of the Budget is allocated to study the monsoon. The 
Committee further enquired as to how many super computers the Ministry had and the requirement 
of the Ministry for upgrading their computing fa cilities, the Ministry informed the Committee that  
they have a total High -Performance Computing (HPC) system with a capacity of 10 PFlops. The 
Ministry plans to augment the current HPC from 10 PFlops to 40 PFlops by 2022 and to 100 PFlops 
by 2024. In response to a further query on the subject, the Ministry noted that normally they procure 
these computers by global tenders. In India, such high performance computers are not available in 
the private sector for Weather and Climate applications. In fact, the Min istry has the largest 
supercomputer in India.   It was also informed that the Ministry needed Rs.1600 crores to upgrade 
their computing facilities. 
5.8 The Committee underlines the importance of the monsoon for India and its people, 
and finds that a 30 percent allocation of the Ministry’s budget to study the monsoon is a low 
figure. Further, the Committee is of the considered view that given the alarming nature of 
changing rainfall pattern s in various parts of the country, which adversely affects the local 
population, and especially the farmers  and the ir crops; there is an urgent need to provide 
advance information about such events to all stakeholders , especially to farmers and fisher 
folks in the country.  
5.9 Although the Ministry has stated that it may be able to make predictions 24 hours 
before such events, the  Committee is of the view that there is a need for the country  to know 

10 
 
the forecast about rains, heavy rains and cloudbursts, sufficiently in advance, in order to be 
able to take any pre-emptive action in the matter.  
5.10  The Committee is of the  view that the Ministry of E arth Sciences, being the nodal 
Ministry of the Government of India in this field, must prioritise study of the monsoon. The 
Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry must make significant investments  to 
expand the network of radars , High -Performance Computing systems  etc. for predicting 
rainfall, cloudbursts,  and natural disasters.  The Committee further recommends that  the 
Ministry must be allocated adequate additional funds to wards setting up of observational 
facilities to improve the predictability of monsoon at the national level on a mission mode , 
including studying the link between the monsoon and the ocean through deep ocean research. 
6. RESOURCE GENERATION BY THE MINISTRY 
6.1. During the meeting of the Committee held on 17 th February 2020, the Committee enquired 
the Secretary about the generation of their  own resources by the Ministry.  In response , the 
Committee was informed that they  provide services to about 70 airports and earned about ₹ 120 
crores from the Airports Author ity of India.  The Committee further enquired to know whether the 
Ministry would be able to raise additional funds by monetising some of  the data and information

“We are planning that, Sir.   Presently, we are giving most of the data free of cost.   That is 
the Government policy.   All weather data is given free of cost.  Even for forecasting, we do 
not charge anything except in commercial cases.   We don’t generate muc h money.    But we 
can think about it.   For example, while sharing our weather forecasting data with a private 
company or a startup or something, we can make use of our forecast.  It can further make 
tailor made forecast applications and sell the data.” 
6.2 The Secretary also informed the Committee that bulk o f the users of their data were 
government departments.  Also, they were charging  a very nominal amount for selling the data to 
the private companies. 
6.3 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Earth Sciences should explore 
monetisation of the data  and information generated through a well-thought out policy, which 
does not compromise the public interest nature of its  original mandate.  Although the 
Ministry is carrying out a publi c service,  if the data is utilised by private users, especially 
large entities like  private insurance companies, such private users must pay commensurately 
for the data and information provided by the Ministry.  Such a policy will help the Ministry to 
generate additional resources for augmenting important programmes  and also help the 
Ministry, to some extent, to tide over the financial crunch the Ministry faces every year in 
financing some of its important projects/schemes.

 The Committee notes that the reasons for the reduction of funds under OSMART 
scheme are once again related to administrative delays. The Committee urges the Ministry to 
avoid such delays in the future so as to be able to justify incr eased allocation of funds for its 
plans and upcoming programmes, that are important.                                                 (Para 3.12) 
RESEARCH, EDUCATION, OUTREACH AND TRAINING  (REACHOUT) 
 The Committee observes that the utilisation of funds under the scheme during 2017 -18 
and 2018-19 had been satisfactory.  However, in 2019 -20, the allocation of Rs.90 crore at BE 
was reduced by nearly 28 per cent.                                                                                (Para 3.15) 
 The Committee notes that the existing monitoring mechanism of the Ministry has not 
ensured overall effective utilisation of funds under the various schemes of the Ministry, which 
resulted in reduction of allocations at RE stage in these schemes. The Committee recommends 
that the Ministry needs to review its financial performance under the various schemes and 

12 
 
programmes, analyse the reasons for underutilisation, identify the administrative bottlenecks 
and take  corrective measures to ensure that funds allocated under various schemes are not 
underutilised in future.                                                                                                   (Para 3.16) 
AUTONOMOUS BODIES 
 The Committee notes that the financial performance of all the autonomous institutions 
under the Ministry has been satisfactory during the years 2017 -18 and 2018 -19.  As regards 
2019-20, the Committee observed that the allocation of all the autonomous bodies had been 
reduced a t RE stage, except NIOT, Chennai.  The reasons furnished for this reduction are 
deferment of maintenance work on existing building and upgradation of existing IT 
infrastructure, delay in start of contractual work of lab, postponement of some civil work etc .  
The Committee feels that the reasons furnished are mostly procedural and administrative, 
and could have been avoided. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should take up 
the matter with all the concerned agencies and ensure that such underutilisat ion of funds is 
avoided in the future.                                                                                                       (Para 4.2) 
 However, the Committee notes that out of the increased allocation of Rs.50.78 crore, 
NIOT could spend only Rs.20.49 crore upto 7 th February 2020, which is 40 percent of the 
allocated amount.  The Committee recommends that the Ministry impress upon NIOT, 
Chennai to take necessary action to ensure that the funds are utilised within the current 
financial year for the purpose for which additional funds were granted at RE stage. (Para 4.3)                                                                                           
 The Committee is of the view that our long coast line is the lifeline of coastal 
communities and therefore sustainable management and restoration of the coastal zone and 
shorelines is essential.  The success of the demonstration studies carried out shows that such 
projects of the National Institute of Ocean Technology must be encouraged in all states along 
the coastline .  The Committee recommends that the Government should pay adequate 
attention to the needs of NIOT and equip NIOT with the promised manpower  at the earliest 
to enable it to carry out its mandated activities.                                                              (Para 4.6) 
WEATHER FORECASTS/RAINFALL VARIABILITY AND CHANGES 
 The Committee underlines the importance of the monsoon for India and its people, 
and finds that a 30 percent allocation of the Ministry’s budget to study the monsoon is a low 
figure. Further, the Committee is of the considered view that given the alarming nature of 
changing rainfall patterns in various parts of the country, which adversely affects the local 
population, and especially the farmers and their crops; there is an urgent need to provide 
advance information about such events to all stakeholders, es pecially to farmers and fisher  
folks in the country.                                                                                                       (Para 5.8) 
 Although the Ministry has stated that it may be able to make predictions 24 hours 
before such events, the Committee is of the view that there is a need for the country to know 
the forecast about rains, heavy rains and cloudbursts, sufficiently in advance, in order to be 
able to take any pre-emptive action in the matter.                                                          (Para 5.9) 
 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Earth Sciences, being the nodal 
Ministry of the Government of India in this field, must prioritise study of the monsoon. The 
Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry must make significant investments to 
expand the network of radars, High -Performance Computing systems etc. for predicting 
rainfall, cloudbursts, and natural disasters.  The Committee further recommends that the 
Ministry must be allocated adequ ate additional funds towards setting up of observational 
facilities to improve the predictability of monsoon at the national level on a mission mode, 
including studying the link between the monsoon and the ocean through deep ocean research.                                                                   
                                                                                                                                       (Para 5.10) 
 
 

13 
 
RESOURCE GENERATION BY THE MINISTRY 
 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Earth Sciences should explore 
monetisation of the data and information generated through a well -thought out policy, which 
does not compromise the public interest nature of its original mandate.  Although the 
Ministry is carrying out a public service, if the data is utilised by private users, especially 
large entities like private insurance companies, such private users must pay commensurately 
for the data and information provided by the Ministry.  Such a policy will help the Ministry to 
generate additional resources for augmenting important programmes and also help the 
Ministry, to some extent, to tide over the financial crunch the Ministry faces every year in 
financing some of its important projects/schemes.                                                         (Para 6.3)

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
BUDGETERY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2019 -20 AND ALLOCATION 
FOR 2020-21 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.1 The Committee was informed that the Department had made a projected demand of                          
Rs. 40,259.05 crore for BE 2020 -21 against which an amount of Rs.26,691.70 crore has been 
allocated, registering an overall reduction of Rs.13,567.35 crore i.e. 33.70% less than the projected 
demand of the Department.  Of the seven Ministries/Departments  under the purview of the Committee, 
it is only the budgetary allocations for the DAE in BE 2020 -21 that is cause for grave concern.  
Approximately 41% of this shortfall amount of Rs.13,567.35 crore is the revenue expenditure and 59% 
affects the projected capital expenditure.                                                                                     (Para 2.2)                                      
                                                                                                                        
Action Taken 
1.2 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee in respect of para 2.2 of the 326 th Report are 
noted.  The Department will take up the matter with Ministry of Finance at RE 2020-21 stage.  
Recommendation/Observation  
1.3 The Committee is of the considered opinion that there are expenditures such as salaries to 
employees, payment of utility bills, etc. under the Revenue head which are obligatory in nature and any 
reduction/shortfall in funds under these components would be akin  to denying oxygen to life, and will 
severely affect the overall functioning of the Department of Atomic Energy.  The Committee is, 
therefore, fully convinced that expenditure of obligatory nature must not be subjected to any kind of 
reduction/shortfall whatsoever.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that, at the very minimum,  
adequate funds to meet such expenditure of obligatory nature should be allocated by the Ministry of 
Finance at the RE stage.                                                                                                             (Para 2.5)                                                               
Action Taken 
1.4 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee in respect of para 2.5 of the 326 th Report are 
noted.  The Department will take up the matter with Ministry of Finance at RE 2020-21 stage.  
SPECIAL OBSERVATIONS 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.5 The Committee notes that the country's nuclear energy programme is at a very sensitive 
crossroads.  From the point of view of emi ssions of greenhouse gases, nuclear power is a clean source 
of electricity.  However, its costs are not coming down.  In fact, they are going up due to greater 
concerns on safety, following the Fukushima disaster in May 2011.  On the other hand, prices of solar 
power have come crashing down and the relative economics of nuclear and solar power has changed 
dramatically.  This cannot be ignored totally, even though presently solar power is intermittent power 
and conversions efficiency is low.  The Committee believes India cannot afford to do away with a base-
load source of electricity like nuclear power.  India's nuclear energy programme has both a strategic 
and energy dimension, and both of these have to be kept in view while considering the Department of 
Atomic Energy.                                                                                                                             (Para 3.1)                                                  
 

3 
 
Action Taken 
1.6 The Hon. Committee’s observation is noted. NPCIL is very conscious of the competitiveness of 
nuclear power and its efforts to reduce its tariffs are ongoing. These efforts include optimizing the 
capital cost of nuclear power projects by standardization of design, reducing gestation period, constan t 
monitoring at multiple levels with timely interventions to ensure timely completion of projects and 
having a fair tariff mechanism. 
Recommendation/Observation  
1.7 The Committee hopes that the DAE would be in a position to commission the fast breeder 
reactor at Kalpakkam by the end of 2021.  Even though it would have taken almost two decades when 
commissioning takes place, this is a pioneering initiative of which India can be justifiably proud.  It 
will transform our nuclear energy programme.  In addition , the Committee hopes that the DAE will 
take forward the plans to set up the advanced thorium reactor on an engineering scale, which is the 
ultimate objective of the three -phase nuclear energy programme, as envisaged by Dr. Homi J. Bhabha 
in the early 1950 s.  The Committee also wishes to draw the attention of the DAE to a recent study of 
the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (C -STEP), Bengaluru, which argued for large -
scale induction of thorium -based reactors ahead of the second stage fast breeders for gaining early 
experience with thorium.                                                                                                              (Para 3.2)                                                                                   
Action Taken 
1.8 Owing to its first -of-a-kind indigenous effort towards technology development, the on -going 
PFBR project has been facing both time & cost escalation. The initial delays were essentially due to the 
delays in systems & equipment development/fabrication by manufacturers. This was owing to the need 
for development of the required materials with specific metallurgical compositions & manufacturing 
processes for sodium applications and also owing to the complexity & precision in manufacturing/ 
fabrication of the various systems, structures & equipment (SSE) of PFBR. There have been further 
delays owing to the need for specialized erection & installation methodology/techniques/handling -
equipment for extra -large & slender components, viz. Main -Vessel, Safety Vessel & Inner -Vessel, 
Primary Sodium Pumps, Intermediate Heat -Exchangers, Steam-Generators, etc. Again, during the on -
going commissioning process, which commenced in the beginning of 2015, many difficulties have 
been encountered, due to first -of-a-kind design complexities of the SSEs in high -temperature 
environment.  
1.9 During the past four years, while  commissioning activities of  the various SSEs (Systems, 
Structures & Equipment) of PFBR are progressing, a large number of technical challenges as  well as 
design inadequacies (owing to the first -of-a-kind status of the PFBR) are being encountered at each 
stage, thereby resulting into delays. The initial milestones pertaining to (a) pre -heating (b) reduction in 
the leak-rate of the reactor containmen t building and (c) reduction in the total leak -rate of the reactor 
assembly, required a large number of corrective measures, since there were differences noticed in 
actual field conditions, as against the earlier estimated values. After effective design mo difications and 
in-situ corrections, pre-heating of the reactor assembly could be carried out and the secondary sodium 
loops were started. However, there were a number of failures in the electro -magnetic pumps, which 
took a lot of time to understand and re ctify. Further to it the secondary sodium pump had also failed 
due to discrepancies between theoretical analysis and as observed behavior of the piping reactions.  
1.10 All these could be successfully rectified and both the secondary loops could be re -started in 
March 2019 and operated for eight months.  During this operation of the secondary sodium loops, the 
failure-zones of the electro -magnetic pumps, had been identified and dynamically adjusted based on 
vibration parameters and the performance of both t he secondary sodium pumps could also be 
characterized. In addition, the Transfer Arm (which forms a part of the fuelling machinery), also had to 
undergo certain modifications (since deviations were noticed in its performance during the trial tests at 

4 
 
high temperatures). Further, during this period, a snag had been observed in the indigenously 
developed Large Rotatable Plug Bearing (which forms a part of the fuelling machinery for location of 
the sub-assembly coordinates) and the same is presently undergoing rectification, based on a number of 
design reviews and experiments on a prototype.  
1.11 It may be noted that many of these failures are occurring during the commissioning of the 
equipment/components in the plant, at high temperature conditions, essentially owing to their first-of-a-
kind (FOAK) design. Consequently, all these equipment failures have been a set -back to the earlier 
targets and it is estimated that, typically, two more years may be required for making the PFBR 
operational.  The present additi onal time requirement has been based on the difficulties faced, failures 
encountered & performance deficiencies observed, in the various Systems Structures & Equipment 
(SSEs), during commissioning, which progressively required further design reviews & in -situ changes 
and thereby has been requiring much more time than originally estimated. 
1.12 Presently, testing & commissioning of the various systems & equipment, required for filling 
sodium in the Main Vessel (MV), is underway.  The initial fuel loading can  commence, only after MV 
filling, followed by purification of sodium & commissioning of the primary sodium pumps. 
Considering the number of stage -wise commissioning activities, requiring adequate in -stage trials and 
regulatory clearances, it would not be p ossible to achieve the first approach to criticality (FAC) before 
March 2022. Further, based on the experience feedback of the commissioning activities and the faults 
being encountered, it would be prudent to have a graded approach, thereby providing adequ ate time at 
the end of each step for temperature stabilization & performance evaluation. Such a graded approach 
would necessarily result in increased commissioning time, thereby resulting in this delay of achieving 
criticality and subsequent power operation.

Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.14 The Committee is also aware of the fact that apart from helping India acquire badly needed 
natural uranium from other countries, the Indo -US Nuclear Agreement of 2005 has not yet resulted in 
new commercial projects with foreign assistance.  Negotiations with  the French and American 
companies have been going on for over a decade.  The Committee feels that at this point of time it 
would be better for the DAE to adopt a standardised 700 MW heavy -water reactor and use that 
standardised design for its expansion programme in an aggressive manner.                             (Para 3.3) 
                                                  
Action Taken 
1.15 Following the fruition of the international cooperation in nuclear energy, work has commenced 
on two projects with f oreign cooperation – KKNPP 3&4 (2X1000 MW) and KKNPP 5&6 (2X1000 
MW) at Kudankulam, Tamilnadu, being set up in technical cooperation with Russian Federation. 
Techno-commercial discussions with foreign companies to arrive at project proposals have been long  
drawn involving complex techno -commercial, legal and regulatory issues. In addition to above, setting 
up of the indigenous 700 MW Pressurised Heavy Water Reactor (PHWR) is the primary focus of 
India’s nuclear power programme and is being pursued. NPCIL ha s evolved a standardized 700 MW 
PHWR design and presently six (6) 700 MW PHWRs are under construction. The first of the standard 
700 MW PHWRs (KAPP-3) is poised to be operationalised in the current financial year. Apart from the 
six (6) 700 MW PHWRs under construction, ten (10) more 700 MW PHWRs have been accorded 
administrative approval and financial sanction by the Government, to be set up in fleet mode. Pre -
project activities are in progress in respect of these 10 PHWRs.   
Recommendation/Observation  
1.16 The Committee believes that by the year 2030, India should aim to at least double the present 
proportion of electricity generated by nucl ear power plants.   It is a hugely ambitious target but it 
needs to be planned and budgeted for and achieved.                                                                   (Para 3.4)  
Action Taken 
1.17 To increase the share of nuclear power generation, a large nuclear power capacity addition 
programme is being pursued. The present installed nuclear power capacity of 6780 MW is expected to 
reach 22480 MW by 2031 on completion of projects presently under construction and accorded 
sanction progressively (including 500 MW PFBR being implemented by BHAVINI).  
1.18 The direction from the Hon Committee is noted and all effor ts will be made for efficient 
implementation of the sanctioned projects.
